summary.text: A 29-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric or medical history and no family history of mental illness was brought to the emergency department by her family for recent behavioral and perceptual changes. She had a three-month prodrome of declining social interaction and hygiene, then a week of marked deterioration with persecutory delusions, religious preoccupations, delusional guilt and auditory hallucinations.

Mental state examination showed a thin, anxious, disheveled woman with impaired insight and judgment. Endocrinological examination found mild exophthalmos and a diffuse, non-tender goiter without other classical thyrotoxic signs. TSH was suppressed, free T3 elevated and anti-thyroid peroxidase 141 IU/mL, with anti-thyroglobulin 20 IU/mL called positive in the text; ultrasonography showed an enlarged heterogeneous gland with increased vascularity and low-risk nodules. Brain MRI, EEG and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. The final diagnosis was psychotic disorder due to Graves disease/thyrotoxicosis.

She was managed collaboratively by psychiatry and endocrinology, starting carbimazole, atenolol and low-dose olanzapine 5 mg daily. Two days after antithyroid treatment began, TSH remained suppressed with free T3 of 37.8 to 39.4 pmol/L; at 45 days free T3 was 8.1 pmol/L.

Psychotic symptoms subsided over the following weeks as thyroid hormone levels improved, with complete remission, restored insight and full recovery of daily functioning. Olanzapine was tapered and discontinued after sustained stability. At the three-month follow-up her mental state and thyroid function were stable with no recurrence of psychotic features.

ambiguities.issue: Time of the initial laboratory tests is given two ways.
